blocks.text: To these Michaelis (in den Fragen an eine Gesellschaft von Gelehrten, die nach Arabien reisen, p. 305. 306.) adds the Syriac and the Alexandrian translators, about whom, however, we must look a little more carefully. That the Syriac translator puts his ܕܝܬܐ for דיה might indeed seem doubtful, since for the six bird names that are read in the Hebrew text of Deut. XIV, 12. 13. he gives only these two: ܢܨܐ ܘܕܝܬܐ. It is nevertheless clear from the fact that the same translator has that same ܕܝܬܐ for the Hebrew דיות in Ies. XXXIV, 15. That the kite is meant by that word is believed on the authority of the Arabic translator, since in Iob. XXVIII, 7 he renders the Syriac ܕܝܬܐ by his حداة [ḥidāh] (which Bochart proved in Chapter 7 to be the kite; whether rightly, I do not dare to decide). [II, 783] But the matter is much more uncertain with the Alexandrians. For the three bird names found in the Hebrew of Deut. XIV, 15. they give only these two: τον γυπα και τον ἰκτινον [ton gypa kai ton iktinon]; whether the Hebrew דיה is expressed by either of them, and if so by which, no one will say with certainty. In Isaiah (XXXIV, 15.), moreover, they translate that same Hebrew word as ἐλάφους [elaphous].

To these Oedmann has recently been added, in den Vermischten Sammlungen, fasc. 3, ch. 3, p. 75 ff., relying chiefly on the authority of the Alexandrian translator; how much that is worth you will understand from what was said in the preceding note. Nor does that most learned man seem to have weighed sufficiently what Bochart adds immediately afterwards about the order of the Hebrew words in both passages, Levit. XI, 14. and Deuter. XIV, 13.

But Oedmann, p. 81, asserts the contrary, producing Belon as witness, who writes that he saw great flocks of kites, and so dense that the crowd of birds in flight darkened the rays of the sun. But, with all respect to that most learned man, he seems to have made poor use of Belon's words. For in the passage Oedmann cites, Belon is speaking of kites changing their abode as winter approaches, and then, like absolutely all migratory birds, flying in great swarms. Here are Belon's own words (de avibus book 2, ch. 28): Once, when we were on the shore of the Euxine Sea, in the part where Thrace lies, at about the end of April, on a very lofty hill next to the column that stands at the mouth of the Bosporus, where a fowler was spreading a net to catch sparrowhawks flying in from the right-hand stretch of the sea, we observed kites arriving there in flocks on a straight course, in such numbers and so dense a column that it seemed a marvel to us. — But when summer comes on, they return to Europe to escape the excessive heat of those regions. But there is yet another thing that prevents us from taking דיות as kites. It is clear from Ies. XXXIV, 15. that the דיות inhabit desolate places and wildernesses, whereas kites shun the wilderness and seek out cities and places frequented by men, as Aldrovandi reports from his own observation and the testimony of many others, Ornithol. vol. 1, book 5, ch. 15, p. 401. Belon too, loc. cit., writes that in Egypt kites are so tame that they fly right up to the windows of houses.

Schneider, on Aelian 2, 46, suspects that the Αἰγυπιον [Aigypion] is the same bird that Belon (de avibus book 2, ch. 23) saw frequently in Egypt and called the black vulture, although it is not yet sufficiently established whether it is the same as Linnaeus' percnopterus. The same Schneider, on the Reliqua of Frederick II, p. 14, observes that the vultur ater [dark vulture] of the ancients is the Emperor's Galeranus niger (p. 28), the Avoltoio nero of Cetti in the Histor. Nat. Sardin. vol. 2, p. 9 ff., German trans. In the newest edition of the Linnaean System, vol. 1, part 1, p. 248, no. 9, this species of vulture appears under the heading Vultur niger, with dusky primaries and tail feathers, the feathers of the feet black. Yet Gmelin too doubts whether it is a mere variety of the percnopterus (which is the Hebrew and Arabic רחם). — But by what argument Paulus, in the Clavis in Iesaj. p. 234, was moved to take the דיות as white vultures, I for my part cannot grasp.
